days.title: OpenAPI document published with examples for every endpoint
days.doneWhen: `/openapi/v1.json` describes every endpoint with a summary, its request and response types, its ProblemDetails error codes and at least one example body, the document is generated in every environment, and the UI for it is mapped only in Development
days.brief:
### Why this matters
An OpenAPI document is your API's contract: what each endpoint takes, returns and fails with. It powers client generation, API tools and reviews, and it is the first thing another team asks for. A document with real examples and error responses shows you think about consumers. `TypedResults` already gives you most of it for free. Today's React part audits accessibility, the front end's contract with every user.

### What you'll build
On a new branch `feature/polish-e2e`:
- `AddOpenApi()` and `MapOpenApi()` (built into ASP.NET Core) producing `/openapi/v1.json`
- `.WithSummary(...)`, `.WithDescription(...)` and tags on every route group and endpoint
- Error responses declared: `.ProducesProblem(...)` and `.ProducesValidationProblem()` for 400, 404, 409, 422 and 429 where they apply
- Examples for the main request and response bodies, added with an operation or schema transformer
- The bearer security scheme described in the document, through a document transformer
- A UI (any OpenAPI viewer package) only in Development

### Step by step
1. Open the generated document and list endpoints missing summaries, errors or examples.
2. Add metadata group by group; `TypedResults` return types already describe success bodies.
3. Declare the error codes each endpoint can really return; check against week 11 tests.
4. Write a transformer that adds examples for create application, status change and the paged list.
5. Add the bearer scheme with a document transformer.
6. Check the result in the viewer and confirm it is absent outside Development.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every endpoint has a summary and a tag
- [ ] Error codes match real behaviour
- [ ] Main bodies have examples
- [ ] The viewer is Development-only

### Hints
- Week 18 listed the endpoint inventory from this document; keep them in sync.
- A generated TypeScript client from this document is a stretch idea; `api.ts` stays hand-written for now.

### Common mistakes
- Declaring error codes an endpoint never returns.
- Examples that do not match the validators.

### Check your understanding
- What is the difference between the document and the UI?
- Why describe error responses, not only success?
- Who consumes an OpenAPI document?

days.title: axe audit and fixes for every finding
days.doneWhen: The axe browser extension reports zero violations on login, list, detail tabs, board, dashboard, activity and settings, every main task works with the keyboard alone with a visible focus ring, and each route sets its own document title
days.brief:
### Why this matters
Accessibility has come up all course (labels, charts, the board, toasts); today you audit the whole app at once. Automated tools catch only part of the problems, so a keyboard-only run matters as much as the scanner. Many companies are legally required to meet WCAG, and an audit table with fixes is strong portfolio evidence. Today's .NET part documents the API contract; this checks the UI contract.

### What you'll build
- An audit table in the PR: page, check (axe or manual), finding, WCAG criterion, fix
- axe browser extension runs on every page, logged in and out
- A skip link to the main content as the first focusable element
- Focus moved to the page `<h1>` (with `tabIndex={-1}`) after navigation
- A `<title>` per route (React 19 hoists a `<title>` rendered in a component into the head)
- A visible `:focus-visible` style with 3:1 contrast everywhere
- Fixes for every finding

### Step by step
1. Run axe on each page and record every violation.
2. Unplug the mouse: log in, add an application, move it on the board, add a note, upload a file, mark a reminder read, log out.
3. Note every place focus got lost, trapped or invisible.
4. Check contrast: text 4.5:1, borders and focus rings 3:1.
5. Check headings: one `<h1>` per page, no skipped levels.
6. Add the skip link, focus on navigation and titles; fix the rest smallest first.

```tsx
const ref = useRef<HTMLHeadingElement>(null);
useEffect(() => { ref.current?.focus(); }, [location.pathname]);
// TODO: <h1 tabIndex={-1} ref={ref}>
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Zero axe violations on every page
- [ ] Every task works by keyboard
- [ ] Focus is always visible
- [ ] Each route has a distinct title

### Hints
- Native elements (`button`, `a`, `dialog`, `label`) give most behaviour for free; ARIA patches what HTML cannot do.
- Thursday's Playwright setup can run axe automatically later; its accessibility testing guide shows how.

### Common mistakes
- Treating zero axe violations as "accessible".
- `outline: none` without a replacement.

### Check your understanding
- What can axe not detect?
- Why move focus after navigation?
- What does a skip link solve?

days.title: Demo data seeder for E2E and screenshots
days.doneWhen: `dotnet run --project ... -- seed-demo` (or a Development-only endpoint) creates a demo user with about 25 realistic applications across all statuses, interviews, notes, reminders and activity, and running it twice leaves the same data, not double

learnLinks.label: Microsoft Learn: Use multiple environments in ASP.NET Core

days.brief:
### Why this matters
Screenshots of an empty app sell nothing, and E2E tests need known data. A seeder that builds realistic data through your domain methods (so every rule holds) gives you both. Making it idempotent means you can run it any time. Today's React part makes that data look good on every screen size.

### What you'll build
- `DemoDataSeeder` in Infrastructure, using domain methods and the real repositories, never raw inserts that skip rules
- A demo user (`demo@jobhunt.local`, password from configuration) with about 25 applications over the last 10 weeks, all four statuses, realistic companies and roles
- Interviews, notes, a few reminders and activity entries so every page has content
- Idempotency: if the demo user exists, delete their data and recreate it, in one transaction
- A way to run it only outside Production: a command-line switch or a Development-only admin endpoint
- A fixed random seed so data is the same every run

### Step by step
1. Write the data as small arrays: companies, roles, outcomes.
2. Build applications through `JobApplication` methods so statuses follow real transitions.
3. Spread dates with `TimeProvider` so charts (week 12) look alive.
4. Add interviews and notes through the aggregate methods.
5. Activity entries come from the outbox in real use; for the demo, insert them directly and say so in a comment.
6. Guard against Production and run it twice.

```csharp
var random = new Random(42); // same data every run
// TODO: create user, then applications through domain methods
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every page has realistic content
- [ ] Running twice gives the same result
- [ ] It can never run in Production
- [ ] Domain rules hold for seeded data

### Hints
- `HasData` model seeding suits fixed reference data, not a demo user with relations; a seeder class fits better here.
- Wednesday's E2E profile will call the same seeder.

### Common mistakes
- Inserting rows directly, creating states the domain forbids.
- Random data that changes every run, breaking screenshots and tests.

### Check your understanding
- Why seed through domain methods?
- Why a fixed random seed?
- How do you stop it from ever running in Production?

days.learn: Responsive layout with CSS grid and container queries
days.title: Board, list and dashboard usable from 360px to wide screens
days.doneWhen: At 360px wide no page scrolls horizontally (except the board's own column scroller), `ApplicationCard` switches layout between a narrow board column and the wide list because of a container query, and the dashboard charts reflow without overflow
days.brief:
### Why this matters
Many people check job applications on their phone. Media queries ask "how wide is the screen?"; container queries ask "how wide is my box?", which is what a card in a board column or a wide list really needs. CSS grid with `auto-fill` removes most breakpoints entirely. Building a two-column to one-column layout from memory is part of this week's checkpoint. Today's .NET part seeds the data you will look at.

### What you'll build
- App shell with grid: header and main; navigation collapsing into a menu button below a breakpoint
- Applications list: `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(18rem, 1fr))`, no breakpoints
- `ApplicationCard` inside a wrapper with `container-type: inline-size`, and `@container` rules moving from stacked to row layout
- Board: columns scroll horizontally with `scroll-snap` on narrow screens; keyboard moves from week 10 still work
- Dashboard: tiles and charts reflowing, charts sized from their container
- Fluid type and spacing with `clamp()`
- dnd-kit's touch handling with an activation constraint, so scrolling does not start drags

### Step by step
1. Seed demo data, open device mode at 360, 768 and 1280 px, and list what breaks.
2. Fix the shell first; everything sits inside it.
3. Convert the list to the auto-fill grid and delete old breakpoints.
4. Add the container rules to the card; check it in the board and the list.
5. Make the board scroll and snap on narrow screens.
6. Check the charts and their table views on mobile; try a real phone if you can.

```css
.card-wrap { container-type: inline-size; }
@container (min-width: 32rem) {
  .card { /* TODO: row layout */ }
}
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] No horizontal page scroll at 360px
- [ ] The same card adapts to its container
- [ ] The board works by touch without accidental drags
- [ ] Charts never overflow

### Hints
- `minmax(0, 1fr)` stops long words from blowing out grid tracks.
- `overflow-x: auto` on the board alone keeps the rest of the page still.

### Common mistakes
- Fixed pixel widths on charts and cards.
- A breakpoint per device instead of letting content decide.

### Check your understanding
- When do you use a container query instead of a media query?
- What does `auto-fill` with `minmax` do?
- Why does the board scroll on its own?

days.learn: A test environment for end-to-end runs
days.title: Test profile with its own database, reset before each E2E run
days.doneWhen: Running the API with `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=E2E` uses its own `JobHunt_E2E` database, raised rate limits and no background workers, and one command drops, migrates and seeds that database before an E2E run

learnLinks.label: Microsoft Learn: Use multiple environments in ASP.NET Core
Microsoft Learn: Testing against your production database system

days.brief:
### Why this matters
End-to-end tests drive the real app, so they need a real API and database, but never your dev data. A dedicated environment with its own database, reset before each run, makes E2E results repeatable. Turning off background workers removes timing noise: a reminder job firing mid-test is a flaky test waiting to happen. Today's React part designs what users see while data loads.

### What you'll build
- `appsettings.E2E.json`: database `JobHunt_E2E`, rate limits raised (week 13), Hangfire server, outbox publisher and consumer off, Redis optional with the database fallback (week 13)
- The SignalR hub still on, so Friday's live-update test works
- A reset command (a switch such as `--reset-e2e`, or a small script) that drops the database, applies migrations and runs Tuesday's seeder, refusing to run outside `E2E`
- Docker SQL Server (the same image as Testcontainers) as the E2E database server
- A note in `TESTING.md` on how to start the E2E stack

### Step by step
1. List what must differ in `E2E` and why, one line each.
2. Write the settings file and check each switch actually disables its worker.
3. Write the reset: `EnsureDeletedAsync`, `MigrateAsync`, seed.
4. Guard it: the reset exits with an error unless the environment is `E2E`.
5. Run the reset twice and start the API in `E2E`.
6. Log in as the demo user against it.

```csharp
if (args.Contains("--reset-e2e"))
{
    if (!app.Environment.IsEnvironment("E2E")) throw new InvalidOperationException("E2E only");
    // TODO: drop, migrate, seed, then exit
}
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] E2E never touches the dev database
- [ ] The reset refuses to run elsewhere
- [ ] No background job runs during E2E
- [ ] One command prepares a clean database

### Hints
- Thursday's Playwright config runs this reset in a global setup.
- Migrations, not `EnsureCreated`, so E2E tests the same schema path as production.

### Common mistakes
- A reset that can run against any connection string.
- Leaving the reminder job on, so E2E sees surprise toasts.

### Check your understanding
- Why a separate environment instead of flags on Development?
- Why reset before the run, not after?
- Why turn off background workers?

days.title: Skeleton loaders and helpful empty states on every page
days.doneWhen: Every page shows a skeleton matching its final layout after a short delay, first-run and no-results empty states differ and each offers a useful action, and with Slow 3G throttling no page is ever blank or jumps when data arrives
days.brief:
### Why this matters
A blank screen feels broken; a spinner says "wait" but not "for what"; content that jumps when data arrives makes people misclick. Skeletons shaped like the real layout set expectations and prevent layout shift. Empty states are the first thing a new user sees, so they should explain the page and offer the next step. Today's .NET part makes repeatable E2E data; this makes waiting feel calm.

### What you'll build
- `Skeleton` primitives (line, block, card) and page skeletons for list, detail, board, dashboard and activity
- A 200 ms delay before skeletons show, so fast loads do not flash
- `aria-busy` on loading regions and visually hidden "Loading applications" text
- A thin global progress bar from `useNavigation().state` for loader navigations
- Empty states: first run ("Add your first application"), no results ("Clear filters"), errors with Try again and the week 16 reference
- A microcopy pass: verbs on buttons ("Save application"), calm specific errors
- Shimmer disabled under `prefers-reduced-motion`

### Step by step
1. Throttle to Slow 3G and click through every page; note blanks and jumps.
2. Build primitives, then one page skeleton at a time, matching real heights.
3. Add the delay with a small hook or a CSS animation delay.
4. Wire the progress bar in the root layout.
5. Split first-run from no-results; the list knows whether filters are active (week 5).
6. Rewrite button and error text; read each screen aloud.

```tsx
if (query.isPending) return <ApplicationsSkeleton />;
if (query.data.items.length === 0)
  return hasFilters ? <NoResults onClear={clearFilters} /> : <FirstRun />;
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] No blank screens on slow networks
- [ ] Content does not jump on load
- [ ] Two distinct empty states with actions
- [ ] Reduced motion is respected

### Hints
- `isPending` is true only with no data yet; with cached data, show data, not a skeleton.
- Week 16's web vitals give you CLS numbers before and after.

### Common mistakes
- A skeleton that looks nothing like the final layout.
- One generic "No data" message everywhere.

### Check your understanding
- Why delay skeletons slightly?
- How do skeletons reduce layout shift?
- What should an empty state contain?

days.title: Health checks for SQL Server, Redis and RabbitMQ
days.doneWhen: `/health/live` answers 200 without touching dependencies, `/health/ready` reports SQL Server, Redis and RabbitMQ separately as JSON, stopping Redis makes it `Degraded` while stopping SQL Server makes it `Unhealthy` with 503, and the week 1 `/health` still works

learnLinks.label: Microsoft Learn: Health checks in ASP.NET Core

days.brief:
### Why this matters
Orchestrators and load balancers ask two questions: is the process alive (restart it if not), and is it ready for traffic (stop sending requests if not)? Mixing them up causes restart loops when a database blips. Health checks per dependency also tell you, at a glance, what is broken. Week 20's compose file and cloud deploy depend on these. Today's React part writes the E2E tests that need a ready stack.

### What you'll build
- `AddHealthChecks()` with:
  - a database check (`AddDbContextCheck<JobHuntDbContext>()` from the EF Core health checks package), tag `ready`
  - Redis and RabbitMQ checks (small custom `IHealthCheck` classes, or community packages), tag `ready`, failing as `Degraded`
- `/health/live` with a predicate that runs no checks
- `/health/ready` running checks tagged `ready`, with a JSON response writer listing each check's status and duration
- Both anonymous, both without sensitive details

### Step by step
1. Write down which failures should restart the app (none of the dependencies) and which should stop traffic (SQL Server).
2. Register the checks; give Redis and RabbitMQ a short timeout.
3. Map the two endpoints with different predicates.
4. Write a response writer: name, status, duration; no connection strings or exception messages.
5. Stop each container in turn and read `/health/ready`.
6. Keep week 1's `/health` (status, version, environment) for humans.

```csharp
app.MapHealthChecks("/health/ready", new HealthCheckOptions
{
    Predicate = c => c.Tags.Contains("ready"),
    // TODO: JSON response writer
});
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Liveness never depends on external services
- [ ] Readiness reports each dependency
- [ ] Redis down is degraded, SQL down is unhealthy
- [ ] No secrets or exception details in the output

### Hints
- Redis and RabbitMQ have fallbacks or retries in JobHunt, so the app still serves requests without them.
- Friday's smoke test calls `/health/ready` first.

### Common mistakes
- A liveness check that pings the database, causing restarts during a database blip.
- Returning exception messages to anonymous callers.

### Check your understanding
- Liveness vs readiness: what does each control?
- Why is Redis degraded, not unhealthy?
- What must health output never contain?

days.learn: Playwright: locators, fixtures, fresh login per test
days.title: E2E: register, add an application, move it on the board, add an interview
days.doneWhen: `npx playwright test` in `/e2e` resets the E2E database, starts the API and web app, and passes a journey test (register, add an application, move it on the board, add an interview) in Chromium and Firefox, with every test logging in fresh
days.brief:
### Why this matters
Only an end-to-end test proves the layers work together in a real browser: cookies, refresh, routing, the board. Playwright's role-based locators and auto-waiting make these tests readable and stable. It uses the E2E environment from Wednesday's .NET part and the health check from today's.

### What you'll build
- `e2e/` at the repo root with its own `package.json`, created with `npm init playwright@latest`
- `playwright.config.ts`: `webServer` entries for the API (environment `E2E`, ready when `/health/ready` answers) and the web app, `baseURL`, Chromium and Firefox projects
- A global setup running Wednesday's reset command
- A `loggedInPage` fixture that registers a unique user through `page.request` (so the refresh cookie lands in that browser context), then opens the app
- `journey.spec.ts` using `getByRole` and `getByLabel` only

### Step by step
1. Plan each journey step with a role-based locator before writing code.
2. Set up the folder, config and two web servers. Reuse running servers locally, never in CI.
3. Write the global setup.
4. Write the fixture with a fresh email per test (`crypto.randomUUID()`).
5. Move the card with the week 10 keyboard controls; they are deterministic, unlike mouse drags.
6. Assert what users see with web-first assertions (`toBeVisible`, `toHaveText`).
7. Add a root `test:e2e` script.

```ts
export const test = base.extend<{ loggedInPage: Page }>({
  loggedInPage: async ({ page }, use) => {
    // TODO: register and log in via page.request, goto("/applications")
    await use(page);
  },
});
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The journey passes in two browsers
- [ ] Every test has its own user
- [ ] No CSS selectors or test ids
- [ ] One command runs everything

### Hints
- Sharing one saved `storageState` is the usual advice, but week 8's rotation would see the second use of the same refresh token as reuse and revoke the session. Logging in fresh per test avoids that; write it in `TESTING.md`.
- Test the register form once in the UI; fixtures can use the API.

### Common mistakes
- `page.waitForTimeout` instead of web-first assertions.
- Tests that depend on each other's data or order.

### Check your understanding
- Why does a shared session break with refresh token rotation?
- Why prefer role-based locators?
- Why move the card with the keyboard in tests?

days.title: A smoke test script hitting health and one read endpoint
days.doneWhen: `scripts/smoke.sh` (or `.ps1`) takes a base URL, checks `/health/ready`, logs in as a smoke user from environment variables and reads `/api/applications`, exits non-zero on any failure, runs green against the local stack, and the PR "Polish + E2E" is open

learnLinks.label: Microsoft Learn: Health checks in ASP.NET Core

days.brief:
### Why this matters
A deploy that "succeeded" can still be broken: a missing secret, a failed migration, a bad connection string. A smoke test is a tiny, fast check run right after every deploy, hitting the few things that must work. If it fails, you roll back before users notice. Week 20's pipeline runs this script. This closes the .NET side of the PR "Polish + E2E".

### What you'll build
- `scripts/smoke.sh` (bash with `curl`) or `smoke.ps1`, or a Playwright API test in `/e2e`; pick one and write why
- Input: base URL argument; smoke user email and password from environment variables, never in the script
- Steps: `/health/ready` is 200; login returns a token; `GET /api/applications?pageSize=1` with it returns 200 and the expected JSON shape
- A clear line per step, and a non-zero exit code on the first failure
- A smoke user seeded in each environment (Tuesday's seeder can create it outside Production; production gets one created once by hand)
- The script documented in the README

### Step by step
1. Decide what "the app works" means in three checks.
2. Write the health step with a short retry loop: a fresh deploy may need seconds to become ready.
3. Write the login step and extract the token.
4. Write the read step and check one field of the response.
5. Run it against the local stack, then break it (wrong password, stopped database) and watch it fail.
6. Push and open the PR "Polish + E2E"; merge after today's React part.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Runs in under 30 seconds
- [ ] Fails loudly with a non-zero exit code
- [ ] No credentials in the script or repo
- [ ] Read-only: it never writes data

### Hints
- The rate limit on login (week 13) applies to the smoke test too; one login per run is fine.
- A smoke test is not an E2E suite: keep it to the critical path.

### Common mistakes
- Smoke tests that create data in production.
- Ignoring the exit code, so a failure looks like success in CI.

### Check your understanding
- What is the difference between a smoke test and an E2E test?
- Why read-only?
- What should happen when the smoke test fails after a deploy?

days.learn: Flaky tests: waiting correctly, traces, retries
days.title: Run E2E three times green; fix flakiness with traces
days.doneWhen: `npx playwright test --repeat-each=3` passes with zero retries, a live-update test with two pages in one context passes, every flake you met is explained in the PR with the trace that showed it, and PR "Polish + E2E" is merged
days.brief:
### Why this matters
A test that fails one run in ten teaches the team to ignore red builds. Flakiness has causes: asserting before a refetch finished, a toast covering a button, shared data. Playwright traces record every action, DOM snapshot and network call, so you can see the cause instead of guessing. Retries hide flakes; finding them is the skill. It ends the week with the PR "Polish + E2E", together with today's .NET part.

### What you'll build
- `trace: "on-first-retry"`, screenshots on failure, `retries` of 2 in CI and 0 locally
- `realtime.spec.ts`: two pages in one browser context (like two tabs sharing the refresh cookie), move a card in one, assert it moves in the other (week 15)
- `--repeat-each=3` runs until green with no retries
- A flake log in the PR: symptom, trace evidence, cause, fix
- `TESTING.md` updated with the E2E layer

### Step by step
1. Run with `--repeat-each=3` and note any failure.
2. Open the trace with `npx playwright show-trace` and step through actions, snapshots, network and console.
3. Fix causes, not symptoms: wait for the specific response or use a web-first assertion; never a fixed sleep.
4. Write the realtime spec with `context.newPage()`.
5. Run three times in a row: all green, no retries.
6. Run all builds and tests, push, review and merge PR "Polish + E2E".

```ts
test("board updates in another tab", async ({ loggedInPage: a, context }) => {
  const b = await context.newPage();
  // TODO: open the board in both, move in a, expect the card in b's new column
});
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Three consecutive green runs with zero retries
- [ ] The realtime test passes
- [ ] Each flake has a written cause
- [ ] PR "Polish + E2E" is merged

### Hints
- Playwright marks tests that pass only on retry as flaky; treat that as a failure to investigate.
- Two pages in one context share cookies like tabs; two contexts are like two browsers.

### Common mistakes
- Raising timeouts until the flake disappears.
- Turning on retries locally and calling it fixed.

### Check your understanding
- What does a trace show that a screenshot does not?
- Why are retries dangerous as a fix?
- Why one context for the realtime test?

days.title: Build a two-column to one-column responsive layout with CSS grid from memory, and write one Playwright test from scratch
days.brief:
### The drill
Build a two-column to one-column responsive layout with CSS grid from memory, and write one Playwright test from scratch, in 30 minutes.

### Rules
- A new empty folder outside the JobHunt repo: a plain HTML page or a tiny Vite app.
- Part 1 (about 12 minutes): the layout. Part 2 (about 18 minutes): `npm init playwright@latest` and one test against your page.
- Docs allowed, but try without first and note every lookup. No AI assistants, no copying from JobHunt.

### Must include
- Part 1: a sidebar and main area side by side on wide screens, stacked below a width you choose, using `grid-template-columns` and one media or container query
- A card list inside main using `repeat(auto-fill, minmax(...))` with no breakpoints
- No horizontal scroll at 360px
- Part 2: a `webServer` or `baseURL` in the config
- A test that opens the page, finds a heading and a button by role, clicks, and asserts visible text with a web-first assertion
- No fixed waits

### Self-check
- [ ] Finished within 30 minutes
- [ ] The layout switches at the width you chose
- [ ] Explained container vs media queries in one sentence
- [ ] The test uses `getByRole`
- [ ] Explained why JobHunt's E2E tests log in fresh each time
- [ ] Zero lookups, or a list of exactly what to review

### If you got stuck
- OpenAPI: Monday, .NET part. Seeding: Tuesday, .NET part.
- E2E environment: Wednesday, .NET part. Health checks: Thursday, .NET part.
- Accessibility: Monday, React part. Grid and container queries: Tuesday, React part.
- Playwright: Thursday, React part. Flakiness: Friday, React part.
